text: Coffee report. Eleven spoonfuls left in the tin, and it's a long way to Saturday. So it's one level spoon a mug now, not the heaped one. I can taste the difference. Mostly I can taste the water.
I've started running the grounds through twice. The second brew comes out the colour of weak tea. Gerrit watched me drink it and looked away, and this is a bird who eats things off the anchor chain.
[quietly] Rationing the coffee now. Half a mug till Saturday. Bear with me.

You can tell how the week's going by the sound of the coffee tin. On Sunday it doesn't make a sound, it's that full. By now it rattles, and I count. Twelve spoonfuls, then nine, then sums, and the sums never come out well. So the evening mug goes first, and the afternoon one gets thinner. [sighs] It's not a hardship. It's just that a man without coffee talks slower, and you'll have noticed.
Station rule number nine: the last spoonful in the tin is not for drinking. It's for Saturday, before the row. I made that rule myself, on a full tin. I'm thinking of appealing it.

Saturday, so it's the supply run. The dinghy's bailed, the empty jerrycans are in, and the list's in my pocket: coffee, diesel, tins, and a record if there is one. While I'm gone you'll get the station on cassette, an hour of me I put on tape during the week. If I sound a bit flat on it... that was Thursday's coffee. Or Thursday's lack of it.

The harbour on a Saturday is all elbows. Boats unloading, somebody painting a hull upside down, a dog that's in charge of the fuel pontoon. I tie up at the far end, by the slipway, and keep my head down, because the harbourmaster has a clipboard and a long memory. He wants to know where I'm moored. I always tell him: out there. And I point. It's true.

There's a harbourmaster on the mainland who would very much like to know what the aerial on my boat is for. So on Saturdays I come in behind the fishing boats, buy what I need, and cast off before he's finished his lunch. Twenty minutes, rope to rope. I'm getting quicker. So is he.

What I traded today: a cassette of the show and two tins of peaches, for a bag of coffee beans and a fan belt that might fit Opa. The fisherman wanted the peaches more than the cassette. [mutters] I'm choosing not to read anything into that.

Back aboard, and the dinghy came home lower in the water than she left: diesel, tins, a full bag of coffee, and one record from the box at the back of the shop. The sleeve's gone soft, and somebody's written their name on it in pen. I don't know who they were. I'll play it later, after the first proper mug since Wednesday. Priorities. [warmly] Gerrit met me at the ladder. He was there for the fish, but he was there.
Back from the mainland. Coffee's in, diesel's in, and the cassette played right to the end without me. [dryly] Nobody seems to have noticed I was gone.
The tin is full. I opened it just to smell it. Then I made a mug with a heaped spoon, and a second one, because I could. It's the small things. It's mostly the coffee.
Full tin, strong coffee. If I'm talking a bit faster today, that's why. Sorry.

Fresh coffee puts me in a generous mood, so Gerrit got the whole mackerel today instead of the half. He didn't say thank you. He never does. But he stayed up on the roof through two whole records, and from him that's practically a card.
Opa's running sweet this week. A steady chug down below, not a cough in it. I keep going down to check, which is silly. He's fine. I just like hearing him fine.
Generator report: Opa is purring. Not a cough all day. I don't trust it, but I'll take it.

When Opa's running well you stop hearing him. That's the strange thing. He's the loudest thing on the boat, and on a good week he disappears into the floor, like a fridge, or a clock. You only notice him again when he coughs. So these are the quiet weeks. I top him up, check his oil, wipe him down out of habit, and say thank you out of something else. He doesn't answer. He's busy.
Opa's got a cough again. Just a little one, now and then, down below. Could be nothing. It's never nothing.
He's worse today. Opa coughs, misses a beat, catches himself. I went down and had a good look and couldn't see anything wrong, which is the worst kind of wrong. [quietly] Come on, old man.

I sat down below with Opa for a while just now. Torch, spanner, rag. I told him there might be a part for him on the next supply run, if he can hold on till then. He coughed. I'm taking that as a yes.

That little hiccup in the last record was Opa. He's been coughing on and off, and now there's a sort of shudder after it, as if he's surprised himself. What he needs is a part, and the part is a long row away. So until then we're running light: lamp off, heater off, kettle only when it counts. Everything for the transmitter. [quietly] If the station goes quiet for a bit, you'll know why. I won't let it.
[mutters] That cough again. [to Gerrit] Don't look at me like that. He's old. So are you.

Opa's mended. A little rubber seal from the shop at the harbour, the size of a coin, and the cough's gone. All that worry, and it was a coin's worth. I knew it would be. I said so, to nobody, several times.
Hear that? Nothing. That's Opa, not coughing. [fondly] Best sound on the boat.

Fitted the new part with Opa still warm and my knuckles still sore. Out with the old seal, in with the new, everything back the way it was. He started on the first pull and settled into a chug as if nothing had happened. That's Opa: he never thanks you, he just carries on, which comes to the same thing. I've told Gerrit I fixed it on my own. [amused] He was there. He'll back me up.

Gerrit's sulking. He's been sat at the far end of the bow with his back to the wheelhouse all day. As far as I can tell, it's about the mackerel. It was a small mackerel. I didn't catch it small on purpose.
[to Gerrit] You can come back up on the roof, you know. [flatly] He can hear me. He's choosing not to.

The good thing about Gerrit in a mood is the signal. He won't go near the aerial, so it's clean as glass. The bad thing is he's been taking it out on the tarp. I won't go into it. Somebody has to scrub that tarp, and it won't be the one who's sulking.
Gerrit's in a good mood. He's up on the aerial doing that thing with his head, and he stayed for the whole of the last record. If there was a bit of static in it... that was applause.
Gerrit brought me a fish today. Half a fish. [quietly] I'll take it.

No idea what's got into Gerrit. He walked into the wheelhouse, had a look at the record player, and sat down by my chair like a dog. Twenty minutes, through two records. Then he got up and left without a word, back to his usual self. I've written the date down.
No Gerrit on the aerial today. A day off, I suppose. The signal's never been cleaner. Lovely.
Still no Gerrit. I put a fish out on the roof anyway, by his crate. Not because I'm worried. That's just where the fish goes.

You'll have noticed the signal's clean. No static, no landings. Gerrit's away, wherever gulls go on a day off. Good for him. I've had the boat to myself, which is what I always say I want. I played a long record and nobody left halfway. I ate on deck without supervision. And every now and then I look up at the aerial, out of habit, the way you'd look at a clock that's stopped. [quietly] He'll be back. He always is.
If you're near the mainland and you see a herring gull with a look on him... [quietly] tell him his crate's where he left it. That's all. No message.

The inspectors came by today. Transmitter under the tarp, seagull cassette in the deck, me on the stern with a rod. One of them asked what the aerial was for. I said gulls like somewhere to sit. Gerrit was sitting on it at the time, which helped.
They asked whether I'd seen a pirate radio station round here. I said I'd keep an eye out. [deadpan] They wrote that down.

Gerrit's finest hour today. The inspectors came alongside, and while they were busy looking at my tarp, he landed on their boat, walked the length of it, and left something on the clipboard. They went home early. I never trained him for that. You can't train that.

Sorry about all the seagulls earlier. That was the cassette. We had visitors: the inspectors' boat, the same two as last time. One does the talking, one does the binoculars. They asked about the aerial, about the generator, about the cable going under the green tarp. I said the tarp's for my fishing gear, which is true, there's a rod lying on it. They looked at Gerrit. Gerrit looked at them. They left. [exhales] Anyway. Where were we.
